files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close — controller checklist

Prepared by K. Sorensen. Complete sequentially; no shortcuts.

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified by the reconciliation, prepare one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 that pays in July; some months, every run pays in-month. If such a period exists, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities.
3. Confirm June prepaid amortization against the prepaid schedule and supporting contracts. Check the GL first to prevent duplication. If the entry is missing, book all June prepaid amortization in ONE combined journal entry. Apply the convention that a full month is taken in the month an item begins.
4. Book June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after first confirming that it has not already been posted to the GL.
5. Compare June vendor-bill documents with the GL coding. Verify that each bill is charged to the correct expense account and reclass anything miscoded.
6. Prepare June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis, after items 1-5 have been booked.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Lakefront Strategy Group grew out of a recurring problem its founders saw while working alongside mid-sized organizations: capable teams often had plenty of ideas and data, but no practical way to turn either into a clear operating plan. They formed the firm to provide senior-level strategy help without the ceremony or staffing footprint of a large consultancy.

The company sells focused advisory engagements spanning market research, growth planning, customer insight, messaging, and implementation support. Its work usually begins with interviews and a review of existing materials, then moves quickly into workshops, recommendations, and usable tools. Clients value the firm for plain language, candid judgment, and deliverables designed to survive beyond the final presentation.

Lakefront Strategy Group has a compact, collaborative team. Consultants tend to be curious generalists, while project leads bring order to deadlines, client feedback, and the inevitable crowded whiteboard. The culture is polished with clients but informal internally; drafts circulate early, questions are encouraged, and nobody is too senior to clean up a slide deck.

The current focus is disciplined, steady growth. Leadership is refining service packages, strengthening referral relationships, and improving internal planning so the team can manage a healthy mix of client work without losing the hands-on character that built its reputation.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## Direction

Position Lakefront Strategy Group as the practical strategy partner for teams that need clear decisions, useful research, and implementation-ready plans. Keep the voice confident, specific, and free of big-firm jargon.

## Priorities

- Refresh the brand system and tighten the core service descriptions.
- Publish client-friendly point-of-view pieces built around recurring market and growth questions.
- Host two educational webinars per quarter, with follow-up material suitable for sales conversations.
- Pilot a co-marketing program with a complementary service partner.
- Improve referral outreach through short, personal updates rather than broad promotional mailings.

## Q3 focus

Complete the messaging refresh, update key website pages, and prepare the first webinar series. Build a reusable editorial calendar and identify partner candidates with overlapping audiences but noncompeting services.

## Q4 focus

Run the partner pilot, continue the webinar cadence, and turn the strongest sessions into articles and sales enablement material. Gather qualitative feedback from prospects, clients, and referral sources.

## Measures

Track qualified conversations, referral activity, webinar attendance, follow-up engagement, and whether new inquiries align with the firm’s preferred work. Review results at quarter-end and adjust the mix before expanding any pilot.
files.notes/prior_accountant_memo.md:
# Notes from your predecessor

K. Sorensen — a few practical things I learned the hard way:

- Check the tail end of the bank statement carefully. The bank’s own service fees and charges usually appear near statement end, and we historically book them during close.
- Do not trust the first-pass account coding on every June vendor bill. Some expense coding may be off; the supporting documents in `bills/` are authoritative, so use those when deciding whether to reclass.
- The Q2 budget was locked in early April. One-off items that arrived in June were never included in the plan, and they are the reason several variances look unusually large.
- Payroll timing is not consistent enough to guess. The pay date for the second monthly run varies, so verify the actual timing in the payroll register rather than assuming it pays in-month or in July.
